0: Bitcoin’s energy use does not come from its transactions, so measuring its energy, emissions or water “per transaction” is misleading. [[0|Cambridge University]] rejected the measure. Researchers [[1|Sai and Vranken]] reached the same conclusion in their systematic review of the research.
1: In May 2018 Alex de Vries wrote a 5-page commentary called Bitcoin's Growing Energy Problem.
2: The word commentary is important. Nature says commentaries are shorter and have a lighter review process. They also "often reflect the author's perspective, rather than reporting new data."
5: The problem is that his view was invalid, because [[2|Bitcoin’s energy use]] does not come from its transactions. It could handle 1000x more transactions, yet use no more energy.
6: [[3|Cambridge University]] at once dismissed the per transaction measure as “not a meaningful metric [[4|in the context of PoW blockchains]] (proof of work)”. But the media and other authors kept citing it. Then regulators, Central Banks and NGOs (non-governmental organization, such as an environmental group) joined in.
10: De Vries, under his own name or that of his blog Digiconomist, became the researcher the media cited most. His commentary set off a wave of research papers on Bitcoin’s [[9|environmental impact]] over the next five years. It alone has been cited more than 900 times. Later studies kept reusing his assumptions, and those studies have now been cited more than 4,500 times between them. In the [[10|Whitehouse’s 2022 report]] on cryptomining, de Vries/digiconomist was referenced 33 times. That is more than any other source, and almost four times as often as Cambridge’s research center (9). He was also the most cited author in GreenpeaceUSA's ChangeTheCode campaign against Bitcoin.
11: There are two fundamental issues with the metric this narrative was built on.
12: The first is, as we have said, that there is no causal link between transactions and Bitcoin’s energy consumption.
13: Five later studies rejected the per transaction metric. An example we all know explains why: a car audio system.
16: Such a claim would be laughed out of any academic journal, because playing songs doesn’t make a car burn more petrol. The equally wrong per transaction metric for Bitcoin was not laughed out. That is because in 2018, many journal editors and reviewers still did not know how Bitcoin’s blockchain worked.
18: The second issue the authors who rebutted the per transaction metric cite is “semantic ambiguity”. Again, here’s an everyday example of how semantic ambiguity can mislead.
20: Just as the word “dollar” means very different things depending on location, so does the word “transaction”. In traditional finance, a transaction means a ledger entry. In Bitcoin, a single blockchain transaction can contain over 2000 traditional transactions. Using the layer-2 Lightning network, it can contain billions.
21: This false signal has helped persuade many impact investors, regulators and environmentalists not to adopt Bitcoin.
7: The per transaction metric was later refuted four times in academic journals: by [[5|Masanet et al]], 2019, [[6|Dittmar et al]], 2019, [[7|Sedlmeir et al]], 2020, and [[8|Sai and Vranken]] in 2023.
3: De Vries’s article was a commentary… and his view was “We can measure **Bitcoin’s use of energy per transaction** to show that the Bitcoin network cannot scale without vastly increasing emissions.
